Also: 'Haskell owes a considerable debt to Miranda, both for general inspiration and specific language elements that we freely adopted where they fitted into our emerging design.'; 'Haskell took from Miranda the notion of defining algebraic types as a ‘sum of products’.'

named.quote: Type classes provided a uniform solution to both of these problems. They generalised the notion of equality type variables from SML, introducing a notion of a “class” of types that possessed a given set of operations (such as numeric operations or equality).
named.what: Hindley-Milner polymorphic type system (also via Miranda); type classes generalize Standard ML's equality type variables; the model of a formal definition
named.reason: The v2 quote joins a general remark ('would prove to be particularly influential') with a sentence that is about Haskell's differences from Miranda. The sentence above states a concrete borrowing from (Standard) ML. Further support: 'We were inspired by our brothers and sisters in the ML community, who had shown that it was possible to give a complete formal definition of a language'; 'the Hindley-Milner type system (introduced in ML, and promoted by Miranda and Haskell)'. The paper also shows a rejection: ML's module system was not adopted.

named.quote: We were familiar with the idea, in the form of the “offside rule” from our use of Turner’s languages SASL (Turner, 1976) and Miranda (Turner, 1986), although the idea goes back to Christopher Strachey’s CPL (Barron et al., 1963), and it was also featured in ISWIM (Landin, 1966).
named.what: the layout (offside) rule, as earlier origin
named.reason: CPL is cited as where the idea goes back to; the committee says it knew the rule from SASL and Miranda.

named.quote: We were familiar with the idea, in the form of the “offside rule” from our use of Turner’s languages SASL (Turner, 1976) and Miranda (Turner, 1986), although the idea goes back to Christopher Strachey’s CPL (Barron et al., 1963), and it was also featured in ISWIM (Landin, 1966).
named.what: the layout (offside) rule, as earlier example
named.reason: Prior art only. ISWIM is otherwise named as the ancestor of SASL ('a sugared lambda calculus derived from the applicative subset of Landin’s ISWIM').

named.quote: The name of the report, “Report on the Programming Language Haskell, A Non-strict, Purely Functional Language,” was inspired in part by the “Report on the Algorithmic Language Scheme,” [...]
named.what: the title of the language report; one early compiler (Yale Haskell) compiled to Scheme/T and Common Lisp
named.reason: A document title and one implementation's back end, not language design. The sentence continues by saying the Scheme report was in turn modelled after the Algol report; its ending was cut by my text search, hence '[...]'. Scheme and ML are otherwise credited only with promoting the functional style; the paper contrasts Haskell's infix syntax with Scheme's prefix notation.

named.quote: Even at that stage, functional programming languages had a long history, beginning with John McCarthy’s invention of Lisp in the late 1950s (McCarthy, 1960).
named.what: general history of functional programming
named.reason: Background history and contrasts ('the call-by-value mechanism of languages like Lisp and ML'); no borrowing stated.

named.quote: Ultimately, the limitations of basing a Haskell compiler on a Common Lisp back-end caught up with the project.
named.what: back end of one implementation (Yale Haskell), later abandoned
named.reason: One of several implementations, not the language; not a non-design tie worth recording.

v2_quote_check.comment: Both parts found, in different sections: 'Milner’s polymorphic type system for ML would prove to be particularly influential (Milner, 1978; Damas and Milner, 1982).' (section 2) and '...and incorporated many innovations to the core Hindley-Milner type system, especially type classes (Section 6).' (section 3.8, in the list of differences from Miranda).

All three fragments found: 'Of all the lazy languages under development, David Turner’s Miranda was by far the most mature.', 'After a brief and cordial interchange, Turner declined.' and 'It should be freely available.' (one of the committee's goals). None of them states the influence; the section 3.8 sentence does.
